utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Gerry Dobbyn, Marina Vilova, and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Aleksandar Aleksic representing Mr. Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no preliminary matters, could the usher please escort the witness to the stand. Mr. Hannis, while the witness is on his way in, now that you have made a start, what do you expect -- how much longer do you expect that you would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, taking into account that I feel like I need to impose at lease a half-hour sanction on myself for the delay while the witness read a document yesterday and therefore reducing my time from 20 to 19 and a half hours, I'm hoping that I can be finished on Thursday. But I'll have a better idea at the end of the day. But I was hoping I could be done on Thursday near the end of the day, if not the end of the day. Yes, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if that happens, Mr. Zecevic, do you have a witness who would be available for Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, depending on what time will Mr. Hannis finish his cross-examination, I will have some re-direct. At this point I can't say how much. But, Your Honours, we will not have another witness for Friday. Our next witness is scheduled for Monday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the record can show that Mr. Cvijetic joined the Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, good morning to you. I remind you, before Mr. Hannis continues his cross-examination, that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to resume by showing the witness Exhibit 1D547. We were looking at this yesterday. I think it's Prosecution tab 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Andan, I just wanted to ask you, before I forgot, about certain persons that you will have known. Cedo Kljajic, Dragan Kijac, and Tomo Kovac, do you know, are all three of those men still alive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, good morning. As far as I know, they are alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we were looking at this document dated 2nd of June. This was a collegium meeting in the SJB in Brcko. In regard to this meeting, did you send any written report about this to Mr. Jesuric [Realtime transcript read in error "Jasarevic"] or to MUP headquarters or anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a mistake again. It's not "Jasarevic." You probably meant "Jesuric."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And that's what I tried to say, but maybe my English pronunciation of it is not coming across very well for the interpreters. Predrag Jesuric is who I was referring to. And my question is: Did you send a report to him or to anyone else at the CSB or MUP headquarters about this meeting in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Normally, the procedure for such a meeting or supervisory inspection is to send a copy of the report to the Ministry of the Interior. Another copy goes to the chief of the security services centre in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who organised this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of the minister of the interior, I received instructions from Pale to carry out the supervisory inspection and provide all indispensable assistance in order to improve the situation in the police station in Brcko, which means that I organised this meeting in order to discuss some elementary topics. And it was necessary to inform everybody with their rights and duties and tasks. I believe that this memo contains a brief outline of all the tasks of the crime prevention service, of the deputy, of the assistants, and everybody else in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday that there were sort of two sorts of inspections. One would be what I would describe as a surprise or a spot inspection where you showed up unannounced, and the other was an inspection where you gave notice ahead of time that, We're coming to your station for an inspection; is that correct? Were those two kinds of inspections that were done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this inspection, was this a surprise inspection or is this one where Mr. Veselic in Brcko knew you were coming ahead of time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he knew that I was going to come, so it was an announced inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in regards to the meeting, who set the agenda and who made the assignments that we see here? Was that the chief or was that you or was that done in co-ordination between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a preparatory meeting before this one. I don't have the power to appoint managers, not even to nominate them. This is within the power of the chief of the public security station. So we had a preparatory meeting. Since I already knew the structure of the personnel in that police station, I made some suggestions. And I have to say that the chief, Mr. Veselic, accepted everything that I suggested to him. So I did not have any legal authority to choose his associates. It was within his powers. But I made suggestions that he accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were talking about the situation in Brcko, I think on Friday at page 21416, you he mentioned that one of the problems that related to Brcko was that it was a rich area, it was a port area, and so the paramilitaries who were interested in looting saw that as a good target. And you mentioned, for example, 150 trucks of Marlboro cigarettes were taken away from the harbour. Do you know what or which paramilitary group was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I stated this. That's what I heard at the time. Two formations were dominant in the area, Arkan's forces and the forces of Major Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Who or what was the municipal authority in Brcko at the time? I mean, was it the Municipal Assembly or was it functioning as a Crisis Staff or a War Presidency? Do you recall what it was when you were there that first time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite decide between the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, but, all right, I'm going to choose the second option; it was the Crisis Staff. I remember that the president of the Crisis Staff was a physician. I can't remember his name. And then there was also Mr. Ristanovic, I think he was mentioned here already, and he performed the function of the president of the Executive Board. And I think that that was the way that the authorities functioned. However, during that time, I and Mr. Veselic had more contacts with Mr. Ristanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you, I believe the individual you're talking about is probably Djordje Ristanic. Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Djordje Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you have a chance to meet with him personally and talk to him about the situation in Brcko and what had gone on in Brcko after the bridges were blown up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already stated, I had the opportunity to speak to Mr. Djordje two or three times. The topic of our conversation was not the destruction of the bridges in Brcko. The basic purpose of the conversation was to return the police forces from the front line, to reinforce the town with those forces, and to establish public order in town. We also needed to adapt the functioning of the police station to the prevailing situation in Brcko. Mr. Veselic informed him about the situation. He introduced me as a man who had arrived on behalf of the Secretariat of the Interior in order to provide assistance with regard to the establishment of the organs of the police station. I think at that first meeting I did not say anything. Later on we spoke, I made my suggestions about what needed to be done to consolidate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned at page 21420 that one of the first things that you did was request from the municipal authorities to introduce a curfew, so was that the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency through whom you requested and got a curfew set up in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we first agreed that the members of the police should be withdrawn from the front line. The local authorities supported this request before the military. And at that meeting with the representatives of the military authorities, we managed to agree that about 170 people should be withdrawn from the front line. That's when we began to divide the area of the station in sub-areas and patrol sectors, and we also formed an intervention platoon. So those were all preparatory measures. And after that we requested the introduction of a curfew. I think that was the sequence of events. We could not request the curfew immediately, before we had the forces at our disposal who would then control the area during the curfew. We also requested -- to be honest, I'm not sure whether we requested this from the War Presidency or the Crisis Staff, but we sent a formal request asking for their support and their approval so that we could advertise in the media that a curfew would be introduced with the appropriate hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to confirm with you, then: It's your view that the municipal authority, whether that's the Assembly or the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency, was the body that had the authority to establish a curfew and not you in the police; is that right? That was something within their purview?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, we made a proposal and that proposal was accepted. We wanted to obtain the approval of the political authorities for introduction of this particular measure. We received the approval and introduced the measure, and then we announced it in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the police were the ones who implemented it; right? The curfew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Maybe I skipped a detail. We also had to agree on this particular measure with the representatives of the military authorities. We had to inform them that everybody would be checked except ambulances, police cars, military police; in other words, persons and institutions who could be legally found in breach of the curfew without any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, nothing wrong or improper or illegal or in violation of the Law on Internal Affairs for you as the police to enforce that curfew established by the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the regulations that were in force at the time, I think there was nothing unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that in Brcko at the SJB at the time there was just one person basically doing the job of both heading national security and the crime service. Did I understand your answer right about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. Mr. Gavrilovic is brother of a colleague of mine from Sarajevo, Mr. Velavic [phoen]. I can't remember his first name, but I know that he is brother of Vojo Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also talk with him about the situation in Brcko in the preceding weeks or month before you got there at the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you're asking me whether I spoke to him when I was there, in the field? Yes, I spoke to him. He was member of the collegium of the chief of the police station, so it was quite logical that I would speak to the person who heads the crime prevention service. It's a fact. He was also at the head of the national security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 21428, Mr. Zecevic asked you if the name Goran Jelisic rang a bell, and you said you never met this person but you knew the name of Goran Jelisic, nicknamed Adolf, and that's what the top personnel at the Brcko police station said to me. The top personnel, you're referring to Mr. Veselic and who else, if you remember, that you might have heard about Jelisic from? Did Mr. Gavrilovic tell you about him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you misspoke. It's not that I knew of the name of Goran Jelisic. In Brcko it was the first time that I heard about Goran Jelisic, nicknamed Adolf. Mr. Gavrilovic mentioned the name, and he said that this person is somebody who sows the fear among the employees of the police because he is unable to say good morning without drawing a gun. He wasn't of sound mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe part of the witness's answer was not recorded. Namely, Mr. -- when he was talking what Mr. Gavrilovic told to him, he was mentioning the state of mind of this person. Perhaps you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you heard what Mr. Zecevic said, can you amplify anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gavrilovic told me that he was mentally incompetent. Or, to put it simple, he was crazy and everybody was afraid of him. He cannot say good morning without shooting. It was enough for somebody to look askance at him and he would shoot at that person. Everybody was afraid of him in Brcko. Even policemen avoid him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you also hear about Mr. Jelisic from chief Veselic and/or from Djordje Ristanic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did not speak to them about this particular topic. Especially not with Djordje Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Whoever you spoke to, were you not told that Mr. Jelisic had committed dozens of murders in Brcko right in front of the police station, some of them, some in the town park, some on the road down to the river, and many at Luka? Did you not hear about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were not quite prepared to tell me something like that, whether I did not gain their confidence, I wouldn't know. I was simply told that he committed some murders in the area of the Brcko municipality, but I was not told any details about where or how it happened. Yes, it was said that he committed some murders of Muslims. As I have already stated, they told me that he was mentally incompetent and that the policemen were afraid of him as well. So I knew no details. You have to bear in mind the fact that I had just arrived there, so I assume that they did not want to entrust me with some of the things that they may have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But one of the purposes of your visit is to help them get the police station up and functioning like a police station should; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right in the first part of your question. I went there to set up some structures in the police station, to consolidate the situation, to see to it that executives are appointed and that they be briefly instructed as to their duties, and that they were to do all the work that they were duty-bound to do, to process whatever hadn't been processed and put to practical use all the information and intelligence that they had gathered. I wasn't there to tell them, You'll do this or that; I was just there to enable them to do what they were duty-bound to do. I pointed out some problems that were very obvious and just told them how to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree with me one of the primary functions or one of the primary duties of the police in a municipality is to ensure public peace and order and protect the lives of the citizens; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I nominated Petar Djokic for the position of commander of the police station, because I knew that he was a police officer who had graduated from a secondary police school in Sarajevo and from a law school in Belgrade. I insisted and knew that the dispatcher did not empower me to stay there and take up a position at the police station but, rather, to give expert assistance. I nominated some professionals to Mr. Veselic, and as you said law and order had it been disrupted so it was necessary to stand up against crime and other negative occurrences in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had anyone at that time told you that Mr. Jelisic was looking and acting like a policeman, wearing a uniform and telling people he was a policeman? Did you know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you never seen the photographs published of Mr. Jelisic in a police uniform executing a man on the street in Brcko? Did you ever see any of those photos that were internationally published?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see those. I can't deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when you first saw them? What year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At sometime after the war I saw the pictures in the media. It may have been media that are published in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I suppose that's where I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you give the newly-appointed commander Mr. Djokic any advice or suggestions on what he might do to deal with this serious public peace problem named Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably a mistaken interpretation again; Mr. Djokic was not the komandant but the commander of the police station. But I'm sure that I told him in general terms that all criminal activities of persons that were rampaging in Brcko must be -- must be -- we must put an end to them, to that. I told Mr. Djokic as much in the preparatory meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were a professional policeman. You told us earlier that you were an operative by nature. These dozens or scores of murders done by Mr. Jelisic, it all happened within the preceding three or four weeks before you arrived. Did no one bring this to your attention in any more detail than you've described so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if Mr. Hannis can provide the reference or the basis for the question that the murders happened between last three or four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that would be in the judgement, Mr. Jelisic's conviction here in this building, or the testimony of Mr. Gasi, or other witnesses from Brcko that testified in this case. I don't have the page cite at the moment, but I can indicate the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But given my previous answer, I can repeat that I still did not enjoy the trust of the executives there and couldn't speak more concretely about that topic. And I must point out the following: In spite of the good intentions of Mr. Djokic who was the commander of the police station and undoubtedly at the time was the right man for the position, and in my opinion he would have resolved many things in Brcko, he was replaced following an attack on the police station because the persons who had attacked the station demanded that he be replaced because he was one of those who had fled the police station when the bridges were blown up and did not return for a while. So with all due respect, I cannot give -- cannot provide an answer to your question that would satisfy you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, if that's what you know, I'm satisfied with your answer. Did any of these people, Mr. Ristanic or Mr. Veselic or Mr. Gavrilovic or anybody you talked to during your first visit to Brcko, tell you about the non-Serb civilians who were being detained down in the warehouses in the area called Luka, down by the river just a short distance from the police station? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even your previous question and this question here, in a reply to both I can say that it would be logical to expect that the chief of the crime enforcement service knows or has the most information. He should have known much more than I who had just parachuted in, as it were. There was a reception centre, as they called it at the time, for Muslims, and I was told that the army controlled that centre. I didn't have a chance to speak to the military authorities. Now, I don't want you to think that I'm now defending myself, because there's no reason. The only reason is the fact that I was going to stay in Brcko very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I'm not sure you answered my question. Did anyone tell you about that, that non-Serb civilians were being kept in the warehouses in Luka down by the river? Did you know about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I received adequate interpretation or whether my answer was interpreted correctly, but I said that Mr. Gavrilovic informed me of that case, that Muslims were being held in the harbour, that there was this reception centre there, and that the army had control over that. And I said that I didn't have an opportunity to speak to the military authorities about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that you never personally went down to Luka in June 1992 when you were there on this first visit to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in June. And as far as I remember, not later on during the war either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear about or did anybody among the people we've talked about before mention to you another individual in Brcko who had committed some murders of civilians, and this person was named Ranko Cesic? Did you ever hear the name Ranko Cesic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ranko Cesic at the beginning of the war was a member of the Territorial Defence, but by a decision on the 15th of May, 1992, he became a member of the reserve police of the MUP. And according to witness Isak Gasi, who's testified here, he shot and killed two persons down at Luka between the 1st and 6th of June. Did you not hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, I'm not trying to interrupt the answer of the witness, I'm just unclear about which decision of the 15th of May, 1992, Mr. Hannis is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not a document I have in evidence in this case. It's a document that was part of the court file in the Ranko Cesic case. It was a document submitted by Defence counsel in their brief --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But with all due respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's a finding -- it's a finding by Judge Orie and the Trial Chamber that Mr. Cesic was a member of the police from the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But with all due respect, Mr. Hannis, isn't it a fact that you had the opportunity to offer the adjudicated facts from the other trials? If that adjudicated fact was not offered, I don't think that you should be allowed to pursue this kind of questions and then and actually making submissions in a court about the facts that we don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm entitled to ask any question of this witness I want if I have a good-faith basis for asking the question and it pertains to something relevant in this case. And it's my position that this is something that this witness may or may not have known about but it's certainly something that should have come to the attention of the police, and I don't think that's a reason to bar me from asking the question because we didn't offer it as an adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would have thought, though, Mr. Hannis, that the rationale behind the Rule permitting the reception of adjudicated facts meant that if, as Mr. Zecevic has said, a fact on which you rely was not so admitted, then the -- whereas you wouldn't be barred from asking the question, that the -- you would have to, as a preliminary matter, find out whether the witness accepts the premise on the basis of which you frame the question. Is there any alternative approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess I disagree with you. I think I'm permitted to ask the question. I have to live with his answer. And if his answer is he doesn't know or he disagrees or he says that's not true, then I'm faced with the dilemma of, okay, that's what the evidence is and I have to live with it, or I make an application to the Court to either seek to call additional evidence or propose an adjudicated fact, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, but if you pose the question without laying a foundation, aren't you caught by the Rule that your question assumes fact not in evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're entitled to ask questions that may assume facts not in the case yet because when we start out on day one, we have no facts in the case. And, I'm sorry, maybe I'm misunderstanding your question, but I think it's entirely proper for me to ask a question for which I have a foundation and good faith to believe that there's support for and see what this witness knows about it. You can't find that Ranko Cesic was a member of the police in May 1992 based on my question, and I'm not asking you to do that at this point. I would have to offer some further proof of it, but I'm entitled to ask the witness the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you recall my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know or did you hear about Ranko Cesic, who was at the time a member of the reserve police of the MUP, allegedly shot and killed two persons down at Luka camp between the 1st and 6th of June? Did you know about that or hear about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was a reserve police member, nor did I find out during my stay or did I ever come across that name. But I must tell you something else. In one of my reports from Brcko, I wrote that we must get rid of self-styled inspectors, investigators, commanders, and such as soon as possible. That is, in other words, persons who had given themselves titles by breaking into the police station in Brcko and taking uniforms so that individuals put some rank insignia on these uniforms and called themselves commanders and what have you. That's what I mentioned in one of my reports to the MUP. I did not see a list of the reserve police force nor was I familiar with the name of Ranko Cesic. Actually, I think I only heard it for the first time today from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess you've partially answered that. As an inspector doing one of these inspections, would it be in the normal course for you to look at a list of the employees, both active duty and reserve, of the station that you're inspecting, not only to see who's working there, but how many? Is that something you normally do, and did you do that in this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is usual practice. But I had a common list of the reserve police members who were Serbs, Muslims or Bosniaks, and Croats. I don't think that at the time there was an integrated list. I explained how we screened these people, but at that moment I had no such list. It is logical for a police inspector to take a look at the list of employees and the list of the reserve force respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that when the curfew was established that you had consulted with the military about that; correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to reach some kind of agreement with them because otherwise there would be an overlapping of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall who you dealt with from the military, by rank and name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the man's first name was Pavle but I for get his last name. He was a lieutenant-colonel. And I remember major or captain 1st class or possibly Captain Sehovac. We went to the military command on several occasions and spoke to them about the situation in the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversation with any of them about the so-called reception centre at Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't speak about that. I spoke about security, establishing police structures at the station, and the authority that originated from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave Brcko for a bit and go to Bijeljina. At page 21436 on Friday, you talked about the situation in Bijeljina and the two paramilitary formations that were causing a lot of the problems, that being Mauzer's Group. I think they were called the Panthers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, help me with this: I've heard references and seen in documents references to a group called the Serb Volunteer Guard in Bijeljina. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's mention of them, and I also made a note of that. Those guys, those persons, were inhabitants of Bijeljina municipality. They were led by Chetnik Vojvoda Blagojevic, but we didn't have as many problems with that group as with the Panthers. It's a unit of the Serb Radical Party which was led by Mirko Blagojevic, and all members of that unit hailed from Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, we've heard evidence about Arkan's Men coming to Bijeljina at the very beginning of April 1992. Were they ever referred to by any term other than Arkan's Tigers or Arkan's Men? Were they ever referred to as this Serb Guard or the Volunteer Guard, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that time they called themselves the Serb Volunteer Guard. And I'm speaking about Arkan's forces that were present in Bijeljina at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the relationship, if any, that you know about between Mauzer's Group and Arkan's Men? Were they in competition with each other, were they co-operating with each other? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll begin with a short introduction, so I hope you won't mind a longer answer. At that time the Bijeljina Police Station was exposed to strong influence by Arkan's Group. Through operative work we learned that they had unlawfully taken a large quantity of weapons, both long-barrelled and short-barrelled weapons, that had been confiscated from Muslims. They were registering these weapons at the Bijeljina Police Station without anybody interfering. They were taking driving licences, traffic permits, weapons permits from the police station, even blank forms for such licences and permits. I think that there was a link between the Serb Volunteer Guard commanded by Arkan and the Panthers commanded by Ljubisa Savic, also known as Mauzer. It was my conclusion that I drew from various conversations and interviews that they were in direct communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 1D549. It's a Defence tab, 31 I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The usher please hand over to the witness the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, which tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's tab 31, I believe. Do you recall seeing this one before, when you testified on Friday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in both English and B/C/S. All right. I think I need to see the last page. I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you spoke about this on Friday, you said, "We are stating here we will continue the processing of these suspects and submit criminal reports ..." I didn't see any place in the document where it said you were going to submit criminal reports. Do you see that anywhere, and if so, can you point it out to me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the last sentence says that. If you wish, I will read it out to you. "The service will intensify its work on this subject matter and will consistently enforce all the regulations issued by the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This is information stating what had been done previously. This went to the crime service, the crime service interviewed the persons involved, collected the evidence, and, along with a criminal report, handed all of this over to the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I see that what you're referring to. I didn't know if that was meant to include submitting criminal reports, as you stated. I have a question. Some of the individuals that were arrested here are identified as being members of what's translated in the English copy as members of the National Guard or the Serb National Guard. Now, is that the Territorial Defence or is that the Serb Volunteer Guard or is this yet some third entity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the formulation in this document was not quite right, but I'll explain it to you in the following way: These were members of the Volunteer Guard of Mauzer, Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, that is, and I know that after bringing these persons in, we also had some protestors in front of the police station, Mr. Mauzer demonstrated force, and I know that at some session in the Municipal Assembly the representatives of the authorities were asked to disallow myself and Mr. Kljajic to stay in the territory of Bijeljina. Mr. Mauzer asked for that. He said that we were allegedly searching innocent Serb civilians and taking away their goods. So these were members of the Serb Volunteer Guard or, rather, the Panthers of Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You told us on Friday about when you and Mico Davidovic and others had gone to the Mauzer's warehouse and found the three Muslim brothers that were being kept there. Do you recall Judge Harhoff asked you whether you had arrested Mauzer and you kind of laughed and gave an explanation. I have one question: Did you ever call the military and report to them about Mr. Mauzer, because, to the extent that he or his unit may have been under the control of the army, it might have been a matter for the military or the military police? Did you ever contact them about doing something on their own or jointly with you about Mr. Mauzer and his Panthers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I don't want to put myself in the forefront of everything that was happening, but Mr. Mico Davidovic several times at our meetings that were usually held in the evening hours at the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps that was in the territory of Obrijez, I think that's the name of the place where they were stationed, well, Mr. Davidovic asked Colonel Ilic several times that Mauzer's formation or unit be placed under the control of the military. We kept receiving promises that they would do that quickly, that we should be patient a bit, and that they would come to the barracks. As a matter of fact, we asked for them to be relocated. I think that they were also staying at Obrijez, opposite the gasoline station that is on the road to Ugljevik. We asked that they be relocated from there, from that building, that is, that they be transferred to the Bijeljina barracks, and by virtue of that, by transferring to the Bijeljina barracks or any other barracks, they would be under the control of the military. We received several promises to that effect; however, they were not honoured all the way up to the end of the war. So our mission was accomplished in Bijeljina in August, when Mr. Davidovic was withdrawn to the federal SUP and when I was removed, but Mauzer stayed on the very same unit with the same insignia all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan. You told us on Friday, at page 21445, in answering Judge Harhoff's question, about that, that there was an occasion where you actually had detained Mauzer briefly in custody and then his unit set up outside the police station with tanks and weapons, that there was sort of a stand off until the municipal authorities arrived and spoke with Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Davidovic, and you. And you said: "... found a Solomonic solution to release Mauzer." Who were the municipal authorities who came and spoke with you before this release took place? Do you remember the names, how many?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember a particular last name, again I don't know the first name. It's a certain Mr. Micic. I don't know what his position was in Bijeljina, but he did come to the police station and he talked to Mr. Kljajic, Davidovic, and myself. And he told us what his views were and also, most probably, well, yes, the opinion of the municipal authorities in Bijeljina. According to the rules, Mr. Mauzer was supposed to be handed over to the office of the prosecutor along with a criminal report, and we could have resolved the issue in that way; however, a joint solution was found, I mean, in terms of the hierarchy involved, Mr. Kljajic and Mr. Micic. We decided that Mauzer then be released from custody. If you remember, I said then that we had taken away his fire-arms or, rather, a Heckler Koch with a silencer. We did not return that to him on that occasion. When I was removed, I returned that. I think that is contained in the documentation. But Mr. Micic was the one who mediated with regard to this release of Mauzer's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was he the only one or was there anyone else from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another man. I'm trying to remember his name. I know he's a doctor, and right now I do not seem to be able to recall his last name. He was a specialist, a psychiatrist. I think that the two of them then came to the police station, Mr. Micic and this doctor. I think that at the time his standing was pretty good in the top echelons of the SDS. According to some unverified information, he was even a member of the Main Board of the SDS. I'm referring to that doctor, but I cannot recall right now. I can even remember his face, and I know what the man did, but I simply cannot remember his last name. It's Dr. Novakovic, I think. Dr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you say, as far as you know, no criminal charges were filed, no -- Prosecution had no conviction of Mr. Mauzer or any of his Panthers for crimes committed in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when we were there, I don't know -- well, please, bear in mind that there were two possibilities. Filing a criminal report or criminal charges, or sending a report to the prosecutor. That meant that the prosecutor on the basis of our report could start an investigation or redact all of this altogether. I do not rule out that possibility that it was this milder form of a report being sent to the prosecutor. But please don't take my word for any of this. I think that what I have already told you is exactly as things happened at that point in time, although we most sincerely, particularly both Mr. Davidovic and I, were against that measure, that is to say, against releasing Mauzer from custody. Perhaps the wisest solution was found, perhaps the best compromise would have been found, or, rather, if our option had been opted for, then perhaps fire-arms would have been used and that would have caused additional problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if there is no entry in the appropriate log-book from Bijeljina about Mauzer or the Panthers, then that would mean no criminal report was filed; right? Otherwise it would appear; there would be some entry in the appropriate log-book. And I can't remember what the abbreviation or the acronym is for that log-book. I think it's K something.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see that? I don't know. I didn't. So I cannot tell you anything. But when mail was being sent out, it had to be filed in a register and then it would -- and then it would have to say that a criminal report under such and such a number was sent to the prosecutor's office. I don't know. If you have those records, then it's easy to establish whether a criminal report was filed against Mauzer or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But isn't it correct that at the police station there is a log-book where criminal reports are logged, whether they're sent to the prosecutor or not. If they're written in the police station, aren't they entered in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a criminal report was written up, then it has to be sent to the prosecutor. It cannot stay at the police station. Also in the records of the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina, one could have checked whether the police station had filed a criminal report against a particular person. So there are two possibilities of checks: in police records and the records of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if there's no record in the prosecutor's office of having received a criminal report about Mauzer and/or his men and there's no record in the police department about a criminal report having been written up about Mauzer and his men, would you then assume that no such report was ever written?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If all of these records were accessible to you and if you established these facts, then I cannot deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but again, Mr. Hannis, I would appreciate if you can clarify. I thought so far that you were talking about one Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer. And now your last question was Mauzer and/or his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested in Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because we don't know; there might be a number of Mauzer's men who are in the -- in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm focused on Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, not only does it appear that he wasn't charged or prosecuted, did you know that the Panthers guard unit from Bijeljina received the order of Nemanjici at the ceremonial session of the Republika Srpska National Assembly in January 1994? Did you hear about that? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear it. And I don't understand the question about the Nemanjics. Are you talking about a Nemanjic street or some declaration from the times of the Nemanjic Dynasty or something like that? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the name of an award that was made by the National Assembly, the Assembly of the Republika Srpska. The order of Nemanjici is the name of the award, and it was given to the Panther unit on the 9th of January, 1994. Did you hear about that, did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Mauzer obtained a high position, Mr. Savic, also known as Mauzer, obtained a very high position in the RS MUP? In January 1998 I believe he was appointed head of the public security branch of the RS MUP, when Mr. Dodik was president of the government and Mrs. Plavsic was president of the RS. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but then it couldn't have been 1992, as the interpretation I received said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's 1998. January 1998.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, I did know. I'm saying again: Unfortunately, yes, I did know that he was appointed assistant for police affairs and he carried out these duties for a while. And after the killing of Srdjan Knezevic, the head of the CSB in Pale, he carried out his own investigation. I would like to point that out: his own investigation. Without any kind of legal authority involved. And it was established beyond any doubt that during this investigation he used all sorts of methods that were strictly prohibited, including using 220 volt currents against persons. Therefore, he had to be replaced due to pressure that came from the public and all of these facts that were established beyond any doubt. I think that because of all of this a criminal report was even filed against Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We're about to take the break, but before we do, Your Honours, I would like to save time and give the witness two documents to look over during the break, if he is willing to do that. One is from tab 318, which is 65 ter 20145. It's not the entire document. It's only the pages containing photographs of individuals. And tab 308, 65 ter 01967, which is a newspaper interview with Predrag Jesuric. If I may, and could I indicate to the witness what I'd like him to do. One is to read the interview of Mr. Jesuric, and the other is to look through the photographs. And if he recognizes any of those individuals, if he could put one of these red stickies on the page of each person he recognizes. And with that I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, did you understand Mr. Hannis's request? Is there anything you would need him to clarify before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see, so you will be taking a break and getting some rest and yet again I will have to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I'm wondering, how can the witness answer the questions that are going to be based on the interview of another person given to the press? I'm really wondering where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Don't anticipate, Mr. Zecevic. Let's deal with the -- he would have the -- he would be able to review the documents, and we see what the question is at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious to me what the intention was, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I'm sorry I made you work during the break. I promise you that this afternoon and tonight while you're on a break I'll be working. And the documents that you looked at, I'll come to those later, so if you'll just keep them there with you until they come up. We were talking -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one thing. I looked at the photos but the usher came and I didn't have a chance to mark them. That's what I wanted to say. And I read also the documents, but I made no markings on the photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can deal with that later. You had mentioned about the occasion where you detained Mauzer. I just wanted to confirm something I believe is correct. The police have the authority to make an initial decision about detention of a suspect in a criminal case for up to three days; is that correct? You don't need to go to a judge to get that done; that's done on your own authority as a policeman. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 21456 on Friday, you told us about how you were trying to deal with the problem of what I would call a bloated, b-l-o-a-t-e-d, reserve police force and how you were going to try to reduce that number down. And you described for us the operation that you did where you had everyone called in and then ask who was willing to volunteer and go defend the front line. I thought that was a very clever solution to a difficult problem. But you said that the remainder of the reserve police force, the ones who weren't immediately taken off to the army barracks, you checked against the crime files. I just want to confirm what crime files means in that context. Does that mean you checked to see if they had any prior convictions or if they had outstanding unresolved criminal cases or charges pending or all of that? Is that what you checked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The individuals that remained in the reserve police force were checked against our operative files as well as their criminal records. I think there was a dispatch from the ministry that all individuals against whom criminal proceedings were underway may not be members of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your answer you said there were some people who had crime files and, "we simply told them to go away." Is that correct, you just told those upon whom you found criminal files to go away? You didn't arrest them or detain them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a misunderstanding. If somebody is registered as a person with a prior conviction, it doesn't mean that that individual should be arrested on the spot. It simply means that that particular individual is registered as a person who had committed an offence. Another thing: All those persons that we checked against our operative files, of course we summoned them, and we forwarded the list of such persons to the Secretariat for National Defence, and to them we said that their war assignment from that point on was within the Secretariat for National Defence of the Bijeljina municipality, so that's how we dealt with the persons for whom we found that they were registered in our operative registers. At the time, we did not find anybody who had committed a crime and had to be processed. There were only persons who had committed offences in earlier periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Did you in the police then do anything to physically remove them from your rolls, your list of members of the reserve police, or did you have such a thing? Maybe I'm not understanding how it worked. But wouldn't you have to do something to indicate that, you know, Dragan Draganovic is removed from the reserve police as of this date? Who did that, and where and how was that noted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The list went to the Secretariat for National Defence along with the explanation stating that in line with the current legislation we did not have the duty to state the offences for which they had been convicted. However, we did have the duty that according to the then legislation we had to inform them that they were unfit to be members of the reserve police forces and were thereby put at the disposal of the Secretariat for National Defence. That's the memo that went to the Secretariat for National Defence of the Bijeljina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm trying to find out if internally, within the police department, the SJB at Bijeljina or the CSB at Bijeljina, or wherever, were talking about a reserve police contingent. Is there not a list written down somewhere inside the police station of the reserve police, and if so, would this person's name be physically removed from the list at the Bijeljina SJB when you notified the Secretariat of National Defence about this person no longer being a member of the reserve police? Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I follow you. I think that at the time in the police administration there was a department in charge of the reserve police forces. I don't know how many people worked in that department at the time. So the same memo went also to the police administration, with the same explanation that I already mentioned. And the police administration could ask a more detailed explanation for us -- from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 1D554. I believe that was at Defence tab 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's at number 57 in your binder, Mr. Andan. This is a memo with your typed name at the bottom. It's dated the 20th of July, talking about the action in Brcko. And the next-to-the-last paragraph makes reference to what in my English translation says "the special unit of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BH intervened and the Chief of Staff, the president of the Municipal Assembly, chairman of the Executive Committee, and others were released." Specifically who were you referring to there? Was that Mico Davidovic and his men, or was that Milenko Karisik, or somebody else? The special unit referenced in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I already answered this question. That was the unit of Mico Davidovic to whom the unit of Dusko Malovic was re-subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, why doesn't it say the federal SUP special unit, if you're talking about Mico Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they came to provide assistance to Republika Srpska. They were re-subordinated to the Command of Republika Srpska, and we treated it as a Republika Srpska unit, regardless of the fact that they had originated from the federal MUP. So they were re-subordinated to the Command of the Republika Srpska MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you know, were they issued any RS MUP identity cards during this phase of their presence in the RS, that is, June and July, August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Who was supposed to issue them identity cards?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, my question was: Did Mico Davidovic and his men who came from the federal SUP during the time that they were assisting in July and August in the Bijeljina Brcko Zvornik area get some sort of RS MUP identification to carry, or were they simply carrying their federal SUP identifications, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for personal documents of Mr. Davidovic, he had a Bijeljina ID because that was his permanent residence. As for other IDs, I believe that this unit had official IDs issued by the federal SUP. However, I did not see them using those IDs anywhere. One more thing, they also had had the accreditations issued by our MUP without a photograph. It was a simple accreditation bearing number 1 or number 2 without any further identifying data.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Here you're talking about the Red Berets. Are these Red Berets associated with Captain Dragan whom we talked about before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you asked me whether I knew his name, and I remembered; I think his name is Dragan Vasiljkovic. That is an individual who had arrived from Australia in Serbia at the beginning of war, and I think that after the war he returned to Australia and he is currently being tried down there for some offences or maybe war crimes. Anyway, those individuals were related to Dragan Vasiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And even though they had kidnapped the persons described here, basically, they -- it was worked out that they agreed to lay down their arms and leave the territory. Do you know, were all of these Red Berets involved in this incident from Serbia or were some of them locals from the RS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, all the members were from Serbia. Maybe two or three of them were from Brcko or elsewhere, but I would say, percentage-wise, that more than 90 per cent of them were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question is: Why weren't any of them arrested and charged with some sort of crime, rather than simply taking away their guns and shipping them across the border?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether you followed my earlier testimony. I hope you did. There was an armed conflict. This armed conflict, which included the kidnapping of the leadership of the Brcko municipality, as well as Major Sehovac, could escalate into something far worse. And if blood had been shed, that would have been the gravest possible outcome. I think that our actions at the time were wise and correct. We managed to find a middle ground. We sent the list of their names to the Serbian MUP along with the request to ban their entry into Republika Srpska. The leadership had to be released. Later on, Major Sehovac had to be released as well, and we managed to neutralise their presence by what we did. We also had to consider a group that had defected with an anti-aircraft cannon and some other weapons in the direction of Ugljevik. In other words, there was a constant possibility for another attack with far worse consequences. Had we brought them to the police station, we would have been saddled with another problem, and that is the possibility of an armed attack on the police station. So we had to balance all the time between war, in this case war with them, and a solution that could bring peace. We endeavoured to find a peaceful avenue towards a peaceful outcome. It was our joint decision, that's what we did at the moment. Of course, you have to bear in mind that it was war time, that at some times you have to make decisions on your own. In peacetime, if I'm not quite sure about a course of action, I would call up my superior or undersecretary or the minister himself and I would consult them about their opinion on the situation. But in this particular situation, it is you or I who have to make a decision on our own. And even now after all these years I maintain that we managed to find the best possible solution for that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And don't think that I'm passing judgement on you. I was not in your shoes or in your situation. I'm just inquiring. And I want to know if after this happened did any of those Red Berets or anyone on their behalf contact you or Mico Davidovic about what had happened, to raise a complaint or make any kind of comment, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean. After the action or much later?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any point in time. Immediately after or weeks or months later.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except the negotiations that we had with them, I don't think that Mico told me anything like that. Nobody spoke to me, that I can tell you. Whether anybody spoke to Mr. Davidovic, I don't know, but I think that Mico would have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall Mico telling you that Frenki Simatovic had contacted him to complain about these Red Berets being kicked out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. When Mico left the area of Semberija and Majevica, it is possible that he met Mr. Simatovic up there in Belgrade, but he didn't tell me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you know who I mean when I'm referring to Frenki Simatovic from -- he was from the MUP of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I do want to ask you about Dusko Malovic and his unit. The first thing I'd like to ask you is, When did you first meet him? Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Dusko Malovic before the war. I saw him for the first time when he arrived in the police station in Bijeljina. I think he was in Mr. Kljajic's office. Mr. Davidovic and I were invited to introduce ourself to Mr. Malovic, and we were told the same thing that we had said earlier, that we could not work on our own, that we needed reinforcement. That's when Mr. Kljajic agreed with the minister of the interior that we should receive reinforcements in Bijeljina, and that's when we met Dusko Malovic. He arrived with a unit numbering 20 or 25 people, not more than 30, and that's when I met him for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that was? Was that late July 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I cannot remember dates; that's maybe one of my problems. I assume it was in July 1992. But as for the date, I cannot remember that. You shouldn't ask me about dates. I simply know that he came there and I found him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall if that was after the event we've been talking about when the Red Berets were kicked out of Brcko? Was it after that event?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We intervened in Brcko on two occasions, and I know for sure that Dusko Malovic's unit took part in one of those actions. I know that he was re-subordinated to us. So he was in Brcko at least once. I know that for sure. But about the rest, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during your time in the area of Bijeljina and Brcko, Zvornik in June and July of 1992 up until the time you left in late August, how much contact did you have with Malovic and his unit? I think you told us about three actions that they participated in. Did you have occasion to meet and get to recognise and know some of the members of his group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for me to communicate with his people. Of course, Mr. Malovic was present at the meeting when the action was organised and later when it was carried out. At this briefing, we instructed him what to do and how do to it. Mr. Davidovic, of course, led the operation. And all the orders during operations went through him. In other words, I met a few of his people, as I have already stated, during the curfew, during night, when we went around Bijeljina town and municipality checking whether people were observing the curfew. I know some of the people, but there was no need for me to talk to all of them. If a need arose, they had their immediate superior who contacted us in the command and agreed -- and reached an agreement about the tasks that should be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the break I asked you to look through some photos. Did you recognise any of the people in those photos that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have time to look at all of them. As I told you, I wanted to mark some of them. Now I have a dilemma. My wife hails from Sokolac. Some of the people on the photos I saw after the war in Sokolac, and I think that I recognised among them some of the people who were members of the unit. When it comes to those that were definitely members of Dusko Malovic's unit, I will mark them. But now there are some people that are familiar to me but I'm not quite sure whether they were in the unit or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think maybe the best way to deal with it then, is I'll ask you, sorry, once more during the break to work, and next time when we take a break if you could take out the photos and mark the ones that you're sure were members of Dusko Malovic's unit. And I'll work twice as long tonight to make up for imposing this task on you. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. That's not a problem. But if you're planning on working all night, I'm afraid you may not be able to come to work tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to live with that risk. Thanks for your concern. Dusko Malovic's unit, what kind of uniforms were they wearing when you saw them in July of 1992, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was actually their distinctive mark. They had some specific uniforms that were not used by the police at the time. They were greyish in colour. The shades were from dark grey through light grey to white.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In a camouflage pattern?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a camouflage pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of this unit that -- you've told us already that this unit sometimes were referred to as Mico Stanisic's men or I think you also referred to them as Malovic unit, and we've seen in payroll documents Special Platoon Sokolac. Did you ever hear them referred to by any nickname that you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in Bijeljina they were called Mico's Specials. All the natives of Bijeljina called them that because the entire unit or most of them anyway were from the Sokolac municipality and that's where Mr. Stanisic was born. We at the Bijeljina MUP called them Malovic's unit or Malovic's men. I don't know of any other names or nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of them referred to as "snowflakes," I think because of their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't know if you told us or not, they arrived in Bijeljina, do you know where they had come from? Had they come from Pale or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is logical for them to have come from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had they been sent by Mr. Stanisic; is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understood was that Mr. Cedo Kljajic, because we insisted on getting reinforcements, sent a unit out to come to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was Cedo Kljajic already in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if I said as much, but I came from Brcko because Cedo Kljajic summoned me there. He was at the police station or the CSB of Bijeljina at the time already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Malovic ever telling you that Mico Stanisic was the only person that he took orders from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how could he have said that? because he was taking orders from us, too. We didn't go into operations in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and so on and every time call Mico and ask him, Do tell Kljajic [as interpreted] to do this or that. No. We -- they executed orders that we gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned -- Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, page 40, line 19, I believe he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, page 40, line 19: "Do tell --" and it's written here "Kljajic." I think the witness said, "Do tell Malovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Andan, is that what you said or meant to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the context. I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was recorded as - page 40, line 18: "We didn't go into operations in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and so on and every time call Mico and ask him, Do tell Kljajic to do this or that. No. We -- they executed orders that we gave them." And I think that the witness didn't say Kljajic but he said Malovic. That is the only intervention that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Having heard that, Mr. Andan, can you confirm if what Mr. Zecevic said is correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic is right. He is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Andan, I think what I want to do is give you an opportunity to mark some of those photos before I ask some further questions on that. And let me move to something else. At page 21466 on Friday, you were talking about the event where you guys had detained Jovan Micic and some active-duty VRS personnel when they had a truck-load of what turned out to be stolen household goods of all kinds. I just want to confirm: So I understand that basically in this situation, this time and this place, the police didn't have the authority to arrest active-duty military personnel by law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there's a mistake in interpretation again. In the first part of your question, at least that's how it was interpreted to me, you said that he was an active-duty police officer, but he wasn't. He was an officer, an active-duty military officer in the VRS, and he had the rank of major. And it is correct, we had an agreement with the representatives of the military police of the East Bosnia Corps to detain such persons until handing them over to the military police. We brought the suspicious goods and persons to the police station and detained them until hand-over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That seems to me a very practical solution. So in real life it did happen sometimes that police were able to detain active-duty army members suspected of being involved in a crime; right? This is just one example.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, although the commander of the East Bosnia Corps also insisted, to put it that way, that we should carry out all activities provided by the law in areas where there was no military police presence with regard to such persons, because the military police in such cases had to come from another place, and we were expected to make a list of the goods and specify what the persons were suspected of. And that's what we were able to do on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The commander of the East Bosnia Corps you referred to here, was that Colonel Ilic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, it was Colonel Ilic. And a bit later, as far as I know, he was replaced, possibly by General Simic. But while we were there, I'm certain that it was Colonel Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the time you were in Bijeljina in the general area from mid-June until the second half of August, can you tell us, was the SJB Bijeljina located in the same building as the CSB or were they in separate buildings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre and the duty officers were on the ground floor, as well as the legal department. Possibly some parts of these organisational units were also on the first floor. But basically the centre was located on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The answer as recorded obviously doesn't make sense, and it is precisely because it wasn't -- his answer was not recorded properly. Now, I can say, but I don't know -- I think that it is not such a big issue of dispute. The witness said that the police station of Bijeljina occupied the ground floor and the parts of the first floor, and the first floor and the second floor was occupied by the CSB. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Andan? It sounds like both the SJB and the CSB were in the same building.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you told us before that when Malovic's unit was in town they stayed in the attic of that building; right? I'm sorry, did you answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not yet. But that's right. It's a modern building that was opened before the war began. And in the attic there was a suite and two rooms and there were also some offices. The offices were turned into bedrooms and Mr. Malovic and his unit found accommodation there. And Mr. Cedo Kljajic, with his driver, was on the same floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I now want to go to a different topic, page 201472 and -473, you mentioned that there was a dilemma at that time about which CSB Zvornik belonged to, whether it was Bijeljina or Sarajevo. And you said that "in Bijeljina we believed Zvornik was ours." And you mentioned that the minister sent a dispatch saying it belonged to Sarajevo, "however, in spite of that we did plan to carry out a major operation neutralising the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik." Do you remember testifying to that on Friday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zvornik certainly was ours. But the contentious issue was under which CSB it should be, Bijeljina or the Sarajevo-Romanija CSB, I believe that's its name or that was its name. But we needed the minister's approval for launching the operation. We were closer to Zvornik, and the Bijeljina CSB was less far than the CSB of the Sarajevo-Romanija region. As far as I remember, they were -- their headquarters was in Lukavica, which is a neighbourhood of Sarajevo, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P336. It's tab 212.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned a dispatch from the minister about this issue. Have a look at that and tell me if you think that's the dispatch you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that this is the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I see this one is dated the 16th of August, which would have been a couple of weeks after your operation in Zvornik against the Yellow Wasp, so I'm wondering, if the dispatch didn't come until then, how can you say, In spite of that dispatch we went ahead and planned the operation in Zvornik? Are you just getting the dates mixed up about when this came out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, dates are obviously my weakness. I have been repeating that over and over. It's coming to my mind now because there has been some reaction from the CSB of Eastern Sarajevo or Serbian Sarajevo, as it was called, because we were making some organisational changes. And the person in charge in Sarajevo probably was wondering what we were doing, and we replied that this was within our jurisdiction.
