And there was a disagreement about that because a chief had to be appointed and that's why this dispatch was sent out by the minister of the interior. But obviously somebody else signed instead of him. And I apologise again for the dates because it's likely that they will remain a problem while you're dealing with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If Zvornik had been considered to be under Sarajevo CSB and you were planning to conduct this kind of operation, would it have been standard procedure to consult or co-ordinate or inform, at least, Mr. Zoran Cvijetic, head of the CSB in Sarajevo, because it involved something technically under his domain, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement about launching the action was reached in Bijeljina. I know that Mr. Kljajic informed minister Stanisic of all its details, and I know that without Mr. Stanisic's approval, who was minister of the interior then, the use of the special unit of the MUP of the RS commanded by Milenko Karisik would not have been possible. I also know that certain forces of the VRS were used in the course of this action. It was the military police or possibly the protection regiment. I'm not sure. But Mico Davidovic or I could not co-ordinate this with the other bodies. This was done by Mr. Kljajic as undersecretary of public security, and it was his legal obligation to get an approval from the minister of the interior both for the operation itself and for the use of the special unit of the RS MUP commanded by Mr. Milenko Karisik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I take it from that answer that neither -- that you, at least, didn't have any conversation with Zoran Cvijetic about this operation before it took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither with Zoran Cvijetic nor with the representatives of the military or Mr. Karisik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit 1D557, and I think this is -- this is your diary, Mr. Andan. It's Defence tab 59. I think that's in your binder. And I'd like to begin with page 1 of the English, and I think it's page 5 -- or, I'm sorry, page 7 of the B/C/S that I want.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I don't know if you have a hard copy of it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that part of his binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it should be in his binder, tab 59.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't know which page it is. If it's the same that I see on the screen ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's page 4 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's the page that you see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The page has number 22 in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- upper left?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- upper left corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The only question I have on this concerns to the writing in the box. It's information provided by Jovo Mijatovic. Is this Jovo Mijatovic the Jovo Mijatovic who was a -- from Zvornik and was a member of the National Assembly of the RS, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now, but I seem to have added a note that he works at Glinica. I'm not certain, but I think that he was an executive at Glinica, maybe even the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, for clarity maybe the witness can read this because I don't think that the English translation is appropriate of this entry in his diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Andan, can you read what it says inside that sort of rectangle on the right side near the middle of the page, where we see the name Mijatovic, Jovo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Information from Jovo Mijatovic, Glinica" -- probably works at Glinica. According to my interpretation, some of the information or most of the information about the facility where they were making an armoured train and the other combat hardware was received from Jovo Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I want to go to page 6 in the English. In e-court I think it's B/C/S page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your binder, Mr. Andan, it's the entry for the 25th of July, and it has printed page numbers 44 and 45 at the top of the diary pages. Did you find that one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's a reference that says "Stevo Radic, a member of the municipal authorities, recommended that he, Zuco, come." Do you know who Stevo Radic was, was his job was in the municipality of Zvornik at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the source of this information was at the 25 July meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a second. I think that this is operational intelligence that I entered in my diary, and I entered that Stevo Radic approved Zuco's arrival to Bijeljina municipality, if I'm reading this correctly. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said Bijeljina, but I think you meant Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, Zvornik. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go -- we're on the same page in English, but could you go to your pages 46 and 47. There's an entry that -- I think it's near the bottom of 46, printed page number 46 in the upper left, that says "Zuco's brother Repic is in Celopek. Killed 200 people. Cut off ears and other body parts. 150 - 200 people." Wasn't that referring to Muslims who had been detained in Celopek? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is some intelligence that we had received from operatives. It has to do with ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what operatives were the source of this information? Was that civilians, was that state security, police, military, or do you recall who the source was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall the source, but I think that the service of national security also had this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That sounds like rather alarming news. Did it cause you to have some sense of urgency to get this operation underway?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, even without that, without this particular piece of information, because this is just one of the many, this did not exert any pressure on us. As we worked and as we collected information, we needed as much information as we could get, and one particular information that we had received was this. So within our overall activities we had this kind of information available as well. I remember that Mr. Davidovic particularly emphasised, before carrying out this operation, that Repic was highly deranged. I think that he also appointed a special team to deal with him. If I remember correctly, there was a special building that the team entered. And to be quite sincere, there were some orders to the effect that we respond if he puts up armed assistance [as interpreted]. So all the legal requirements have been met, so even if he had to be physically liquidated, we could do it, or, rather, they could do it. Fortunately that was not done. He was arrested, he was prosecuted, and handed over to the appropriate prosecutor's office and further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to page 7 of the English and page 29 in e-court for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I think it's your pages 48 and 49, the printed numbers on the diary. Do you find -- I hope I'm in the right place. Do you find an entry that says "disarm and expel paramilitary formations; see with Serbia about certain groups." Do you find that one? I think it's at the bottom of the right-hand page, page 49 for you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "War profiteers document, disarm paramilitary formations, expel and ask for individual groups, see with Serbia." If I've read it correctly, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. Do you recall what you meant when you were writing "see with Serbia"? Were you supposed to co-ordinate with Serbia about expelling particular groups or particular individuals? What is that about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously there was an ongoing problem in that area where we were, namely the paramilitaries that were coming in from the territory of Serbia. I think that it was necessary to go to the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia with all the appropriate documentation, information, that we had available at that point in time, requesting that at the border crossing between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina they forbid or try to forbid the crossing of the border by paramilitaries, of course paramilitaries from Serbia into Bosnia. Naturally it was difficult to carry that through because the border was open. They could only forbid armed persons to enter the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for those who crossed the border in civilian clothing, they could get both weapons and uniforms at certain locations. So it had to do with that, to present this problem quite simply to the appropriate organs of the MUP of Serbia and to ask for their assistance with regard to further bans on the crossing of the border between Serbia and Bosnia by paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go -- stay on page 7 of the English and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just put a question to the witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because the obvious possibility would have been for the Republika Srpska authorities to arrest and prosecute these people rather than trying to expel them and send them back to Serbia. Why didn't you do that or why didn't the RS authorities just take them into their own custody and handle them as they would have handled any other criminal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, we did deal with individuals and groups, but if in legal and formal terms what you referred to had been applied, then we would have needed lots and lots of prisons in the territory of Republika Srpska. So what we tried to do at that point in time was to hand such individuals over at the border to the Serbian authorities. If they were to prosecute it in Republika Srpska, we needed to have more prisons than barracks. And, quite simply, that was a solution, to get rid of them in that way and to get them out of the territory of Republika Srpska. However, I am not denying that we did detain groups and individuals and file criminal reports against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. But could I, then, ask you, What happened to the paramilitaries that you sent back to Serbia? Was there any condition that they be detained and prosecuted in Serbia, or did they just return over the border a few weeks later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, with appropriate documentation we handed that over at the Serbian border. It was up to them as to what they would do with these individuals afterwards. But you are quite right when you ask whether such persons returned. Some did, individuals did, some extremists as a matter of fact, and then they would bring along sometimes even those who had not been at the front line before. So for a while this was going round and round in circles. What we insisted upon was that they should be placed under the Army of Republika Srpska if they were coming anyway, but they didn't want to do that. And then, let me put it this way: Official state structures did not tolerate that, but some municipal authorities exerted pressure even against us, saying, These people are coming here to fight for their own people and you are trying to get rid of them. That was Mr. Savic's thesis as well, at an official meeting. And I really am pleased to be able to read this for the very first time today, what the Prosecutor has shown me just now. I see that it was Mr. Mauzer who basically held all power in his hands in the municipality and that even Mr. Jesuric was saying that he as chief of the centre was under Mauzer. I remember when I left from Pale to carry out the supervisory inspection we were not interested in politics; we were supposed to do this job professionally. And it is with that frame of mind that I went to Brcko and Bijeljina and everywhere else, because I did not want to listen to political factors. I'm saying this on a personal note now; I lived through all the things that I lived through and experienced everything I experienced. The official position of the ministry was not to allow politics to interfere in our own work, and I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And of course we do respect the work and the intensions that you had in doing -- in carrying out these inspections. But still, my question would be: When you arrested and disarmed these paramilitary groups and when you then sent them back to Serbia and handed them over to the Serbian authorities at the border between Bosnia and Serbia, did you hand over these detainees with any request that they be prosecuted for the crimes that they had committed in Bosnia, prosecuted by the Serbian authorities? Was that a condition for your passing them back to the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether that was a request made, but it is certain that along with the list that we compiled, we did include a brief description of the crimes they had committed. So this brief description of the crimes they had committed and their names were something that we handed over at the Serbian border. There's another thing I would like to tell you. I hope I'm not taking up too much time. From the existing documentation, you have seen that we did prosecute Zuco and his group. Everything was done in accordance with the law. It was handed over to the prosecutor's office. Three, five, seven days after that, all of them were released. So it wasn't the problem of the Ministry of the Interior any longer. The ministry made every effort to work in accordance with the laws that were in force. But you had another problem: The problem of the prosecutor, the prosecutor's offices, the courts that didn't dare to bring that process to an end or didn't have the capacity to do so. But I claim with full responsibility that the Ministry of the Interior had carried out its work in accordance with the law. Now, whether that happened in each and every case or not, that can be discussed, as we've already said. There were some individuals that we sent to the border without having prosecuted them in Republika Srpska, but there are others that we did. After all, there was a war going on. We were not in the same kind of position as one is in peacetime, to do things peacefully, in a cool-headed manner. It was like a fast-moving film, and problems had to be dealt with all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, Ms. Korner had asked me to make an oral application for an increase in the word count, from the normal 3.000 to 3500 words for a motion applying for admission of the MFI'd documents for Mr. Bjelosevic. We have to set out the law and put in reasons applying for each particular document, and we think we'll need the additional words. And that's my oral application. I don't know what the Defence position is. But I'm bringing it to your attention now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we do not oppose. It is obviously for the Trial Chamber to decide on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Order as prayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I'd like to just follow up on an couple things that were said during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I note the transcript -- ah, it now has it correct. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to follow up on a couple of things that were said during your discussion with Judge Harhoff at the end of last session. And at page 53, line 10, you mentioned that you would have a list of names compiled and you would include a brief description of the crimes they'd allegedly committed and that was handed over at the Serbian border when these paramilitaries were kicked out. Did you keep a copy of that information about the individuals and the alleged crimes they might have committed, did you keep a copy of that information as a record in your police stations somewhere so that if or when any of these individuals returned and perhaps started doing similar kinds of things, that maybe they could be prosecuted then, not only for the new crimes they might have committed but for the ones that had led to them being kicked out before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my own documentation, I actually had such a list somewhere of the Red Berets that we had expelled from the area of Brcko. I tried to find it; however, I moved three or four times and I seem to have misplaced this somewhere. However, this documentation did remain at the police station in the -- from the territory of which we expelled such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if -- if we were going to go look for that documentation now in the police station, could you tell us where specifically we might find it? Was there a particular kind of log-book it would be contained in? Can you give us a description of the file or the archives area to search if we wanted to find those particular kinds of documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an answer now as to whether that can be found and whether it exists, but it did exist at the police station or in the crime service. Such a document did exist. Now, whether it exists to this day, I don't know. But I told you that as a matter of fact I myself had such a list somewhere. I've misplaced it and I wish I could have found it and given it to the lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that you had a list, but you can see my point that your personal list wouldn't have been much use in Bijeljina or Brcko or Zvornik after mid-August 1992 because you had been removed from the service and you weren't working as a policeman anymore. So if one of these or more of these paramilitaries came back and started committing new crimes, how would anybody in Bijeljina or Brcko or Zvornik know that this was a repeat customer who maybe deserved to be prosecuted this second time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was removed. But as far as I know, soon after that Mr. Stanisic was moved, too, and Mr. Kljajic left and some new people arrived and had a different policy at the MUP. And I suggest that you ask this question to Mr. Kovac, if you haven't already done so, who was in charge of the MUP after Mr. Stanisic. I'm sure that such documents were kept at the MUP with regard to the policy of running the ministry. Certainly there was documentation available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I guess this is a follow-on, one further follow-on, to Judge Harhoff's inquiries. It was a problem with simply kicking these people out because as long as there was property to be looted or plundered, some of them would and did come back; right? If I can use a crude analogy: It's like in a cheap apartment; you turn on the lights, the cockroaches run behind the refrigerator and under the door, but when you leave, they come back again, as long as there's something to eat. Is that a fair description in this situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, we were a disinfection team in that area. At any rate, I agree that we were unable to remove all of them. We drove them out, and some individuals never returned. But then new groups would be formed. There would be these stories of heroism in the theatre of war. And then people brought things back with them and then the neighbours saw that and then thought to himself, Okay, I might as well try to bring back something as well. We tried to switch off the lights and kill all the roaches, but we haven't achieved our goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's return to your diary and English page 7. I think that's still on the screen. And for the B/C/S, it's page 31 in e-court. I think that's your pages 50 -- well, something strange has happened with the numbering. It's page 50 on the left-hand side, and the right-hand side is page 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's an entry -- there's an entry dated 31.7.92 on the right-hand page, number 91. You find that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. 31 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right above that, I want to ask you about the entry that in my English translation says "Mico, introduction on the execution of operation Zvornik." Who is that referring to? Is that Mico Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mico Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was this a meeting where the plan was discussed on how it was going to be done and who was going to do which particular task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the meetings at Mr. Cedo Kljajic's premises. He was undersecretary of public security. And the introductory presentation was made by Mico Davidovic at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mico Davidovic do the introduction because he was partly responsible for heading up the operation and making assignments, or was it somebody else's job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico did the introduction from his field of work, and the two of us usually worked as a pair on the same kind of jobs. And I may have added some remarks or comments. But as I have explained, I was sent to Zvornik municipality with some operatives, where I collected information about the composition and the numerical strength and so on of the unit commanded by Vojin Vuckovic, also known as Zuco.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who gave you the task? We know one of your tasks was to actually make the arrest of Zuco. Who assigned you that task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was something that crystallised during the action itself. We completed the action, and there was no Zuco. So Mico Davidovic and I quickly decided that I should take that responsibility and that I should execute the arrest of Zuco. I have already described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, you have. And I'll come back to that in a minute. I do want to ask you a question about your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could zoom out to have both pages of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see the printed numbers in the diary. On the left-hand page it says number 50; and on the right-hand it's at 91. Now, up to now we see that the even number is usually on the left-hand page and the odd number's on the right. Just looking at this, this looks like we're missing about 40 pages between 51 and 90. Can you tell us if that's correct and, if so, how those pages came to be missing and what they might contain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain exactly what this is and whether anything is missing here. As I told you, I handed over my diary to Mr. Gregorian on his request. I never got it back. And I think that the logical course of action would be to ask him what happened to my diary and my other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Page 50 on the screen, there, seems to be the end of a continuous entry regarding July 25th. So if that's the case, then the days that would be missing would be between July 26 and July 30. Do you recall writing 40 pages' worth of stuff on those four days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Believe me, I don't think that I wrote that much in such a short period of time. I made my notes on my knees, not in an office. It was simply an aide-memoire. Normally when I would go somewhere I would take this diary with me and then I would go into the field. Normally my handwriting is much, much nicer than what you can see here. I have to justify myself somehow. Look at this writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can understand that under the circumstances your writing wouldn't be the prettiest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's go to page 11 of the English, and I think it's page 57 in e-court for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Andan, in your hard copy it's pages, printed numbers, 118 and 119. On the left there's an entry for 13.8.1992. 13 August. Find that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's a reference to Ostoja Minic for chief of the crime service in Zvornik. Did you know Mr. Minic before the Yellow Wasp operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember him being present as an inspector who participated in doing some of the interviews of the detained Yellow Wasp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he imposed himself simply by being a very responsible member of the crime service, and then my suggestion or our suggestion was to appoint him for the chief of the crime service. I allow for the possibility that there were some discussions between him and others, but I think that he showed a high level of professionalism and that that's the reason for his name appearing here. However, if he appeared now on the door, I would not recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "our suggestion," did that mean you and Mico Davidovic or somebody else made the suggestion or recommendation that Minic get this job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of us. We observed his behaviour and his work, so I'm sure that it was the two of us who proposed him to be appointed to the chief of crime service position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Am I correct that that didn't come through, he did not get that position? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We nominated him. It was then up to the SJB chief to accept that or not accept it. Looking back now, I cannot tell you whether he was appointed or not. If he was, then he would have received a formal decision on his appointment. But I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that time on the 13th of August, do you know who was the SJB chief who would have made the decision about appointing him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names. Maybe if I were to see some documents, I could refresh my memory. I know that we suggested to Mr. Kljajic that all the personnel, all the top personnel, in the public security station should be replaced, chief and the commander and others, and as I mentioned before, also the chief of legal affairs against whom they filed a criminal report. I don't know exactly who was then appointed in the end to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think two more entries and then we'll be done with your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next one is page 12 in the English, page 59 in e-court for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Andan, it's pages 120 and 121 in your hard copy. And on the left-hand page there's an entry that says: "The reserve police force - criminals in Zvornik. There are still unresolved issues in Zvornik - Stevo Radic, former chief Marinko and former police station commander Maric." Can you tell us any further detail about what that was about and what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously during our stay we received information about problems with the reserve police force. The same problem existed in Brcko. And here in Zvornik, we simply wrote down that in the following phase the reserve police force should be combed, so to put it, so that appropriate checks are made for the whole reserve police force. The unresolved issues were issues of the chief and the commander, Stevo Radic, for instance. I assume that Mr. Kljajic had not received appropriate approvals for them to be replaced at that moment, but what I do know is that they were replaced later on. So maybe at this point of time he was in some sort of consultations with Mr. Stanisic. Later on we received the approval to replace them and to appoint other individuals to these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last one, page 14 of the English, and page 71 in e-court in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pages 132 and 133 in the hard copy for you, Mr. Andan. And the right-hand page in e-court of the B/C/S is what I want to ask about. There's something here that appears to be in handwriting other than yours, and my English translation says it says: "Boss. Pursuant to an agreement with your director Rajko Dukic, please give this unit 500 litres of petrol and oil each, and fill up their combat vehicles. Minister of the Interior of the Serbian Republic, Mico Stanisic." What can you tell us about that note in your diary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at the meeting in Belgrade with Mr. Stanisic. It related to my departure for the Foca area. At that meeting the problem of fuel was highlighted, and that is when Mr. Stanisic wrote this into my diary. I was supposed to show this to the manager of the gas station in Zvornik. That would be a way for me to receive that fuel and enable this fuel to be given over to people who were dealing with the vehicles, combat vehicles, in question. And this is the signature of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it this was in conjunction with the planned operation in Foca that Mr. Stanisic wanted you to go on; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wanted me to lead that operation. I already stated other people who were supposed to go to Foca together with me, and I also mentioned the dispatches sent to the Serbian MUP and the Montenegrin MUP. As I said, we did not receive approval from the Serbian MUP to cross their territory. We didn't have combat vehicles. We didn't have any policemen with long barrels. I would not entirely exclude the possibility that we had some hand-held rocket-launchers. So we had some of the dry food and some of the equipment that we were supposed to take with us. Mr. Stanisic spoke to me and because of the problems that had accumulated in Foca, he told me that I should take this into my own hands and that they had agreed with Cedo Kljajic that something should have been done about it. The problem of fuel was a problem that was very much present in Republika Srpska. This is an attempt of Mr. Stanisic to ensure fuel for us so that we could travel to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So this was written in your diary on the 18th of August when you were at that meeting at Bosanska Vila in Belgrade with Mr. Stanisic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was anybody else present at that meeting or was it just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was on my own. Cedo Kljajic sent me to Belgrade alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember now what day you were actually supposed to set out for Foca? Was it the next day or a week later? What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated that I cannot remember the exact dates. I assume that we were supposed to depart during the next few days. We had to establish the unit first, because the unit of Mico Davidovic had been returned to the federal SUP. So from the existing complement of police forces in Bijeljina, I was supposed to establish a unit. I think I already had the core of the unit. And with the additional manpower, I was supposed to depart for Foca within a week or so. But you have to excuse me, I'm not very good with dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. We may return to that a little further on just for a couple of items. But let me go back now with just one or two questions about the paramilitaries being removed. You told us, I think, that the first time in Brcko, that you said 90-some per cent of those were Serbs from Serbia who were kicked out, but you said two or three of them were probably locals from Brcko. Were the locals kicked out to Serbia or were they simply released? because it doesn't appear that they were prosecuted locally either. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely. I think that that part of the fugitive group that went towards Ugljevik, I think that they were mostly from Republika Srpska. I don't know whether later on there was a search made to find those individuals. I can only tell you that those people that we arrested and disarmed, we sent them to Serbia. Others allegedly went towards Ugljevik. And whether they went on to some other theatre of war, I wouldn't know. And I also don't know whether there was any operative work later on to try to find them. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P591 -- [Microphone not activated]. I'm sorry. Can we show the witness Exhibit P591. It's tab 143 in the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I don't know if you will have seen this document before or not. It's dated the 28th of July, 1992. It comes from General -- or I guess at the time Colonel Tolimir in the VRS, and it's a report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the RS. Do you recall ever seeing that document before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm going to pass on that for now. At page 21488 on Monday, you told to Mr. Zecevic that you were trying to underline the responsibility of all those who had committed a crime had to be identified, that had to be established, and they needed to be removed as soon as possible, not just kicking paramilitaries out but also if there were police who had engaged in criminal conduct, that they needed to be removed from the police force. It seems what you've been testifying to, that you and Mico Davidovic were working hard at trying to deal with that issue, but to your knowledge were similar efforts being made elsewhere in Republika Srpska with as much, if I may say, as much eagerness and efficiency as displayed by you and Mr. Davidovic in Bijeljina and Brcko and Zvornik? Did you hear about anybody else doing the same kind of work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to what degree this happened. I know that there were two dispatches orders. One was signed by Dobrivoje Planojevic and another by Minister Stanisic. So it meant that they had the force of order. And all the officers were ordered to work in the same way that we worked in Bijeljina. So the top of the pyramid observed the existence of problems in public security centres. Now, how much did the security services from Trebinje to Prijedor do about it, I don't know. But I do know that the dispatches were sent to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At page 21493, you told us that after the Yellow Wasp operation in Zvornik, that Mr. Stanisic came to town, you had a meeting and -- you all had a meeting and discussion with him telling him about what happened. You described how he was interested in certain colourful details: At the end of this two-hour meeting, the minister said that there were problems that other municipalities were facing which called for such units as those that had performed in Zvornik and that perhaps we could quite specifically be in the focus, and perhaps we would have to count on that, dealing with paramilitaries and criminals not only locally but throughout the republic. Did I understand your answer to mean that you felt like Mr. Stanisic was telling you that you and Davidovic might be involved in doing more of this same kind of thing in other places in the RS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically that is true for me. You have to bear in mind that the period that Mr. Davidovic spent there was a limited period. He could have been withdrawn on the 13th of August or he could have stayed until the new year, so I think that the words of Mr. Stanisic pertain more to me. I'm a soldier of the Republika Srpska MUP, and I consider that if it was necessary to do it, and I think that his intention was that I should do it, that it was I who should have taken on this task on my shoulders and that I should be a sort of fireman who would go to distinguish fires wherever it was necessary to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or spray the insecticide or turn on the light or whatever was needed; right? But that didn't happen, did it? You and Mico didn't get an opportunity to do any more of that kind of work? First of all, he got -- Mico was returned to Serbia, and you, shortly after, were removed from the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Although there was a very concrete agreement. I don't know what would have happened had the Serbian MUP allowed that we cross their territory. And from Montenegro we received no reply at all. And if we hadn't received the reply from the Serbian MUP, we would have understood it to mean that we were free to go. And we would very probably have gone towards Cajnic; however, we were not permitted to cross that territory with long barrels. And after that you know what happened to me. I was chased away from the MUP and I did not have any opportunity to take part in similar activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say, or would you agree with me, that there was a fairly significant back-lash against you and Mr. Davidovic coming from certain elements of the Serb authorities because you had arrested Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I wouldn't describe it this way, generally speaking, but I do have to say that this situation arose in the territory of the Bijeljina municipality mostly because of the reaction of Mr. Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, to what we were doing there. Of course, criminals also have their ethnicity, regardless of who they are. They were Serbs but they were also criminals, so we arrested them and expelled them. I think that the greatest opponent to the reintroduction of peace and order was Mr. Mauzer. Now that I've read the article that you gave me, I most definitely think so. I think he was the one who influenced our stay in the area of Semberija and Majevica, and especially my stay in that area. In some of the documents, you could see that the efforts were made to overcome the conflict that constantly hovered in the air between Mr. Savic and the ministry, more precisely the security centre. Once he sent the invitation to the ministry, inviting somebody to attend the baptism of his unit, and in the office Mr. Cedo Kljajic said that it would be best if some of the police members would attend this baptism celebration. We agreed that Mr. Sinisa Karan, I, and somebody else should go and attend this baptism. And even there, at this celebration, there was something unpleasant for us. I reported about it, and I think that Sinisa Karan also reported about it. In front of a full hall, Mr. Mauzer highlighted me and Mico Davidovic, calling us communists who came to the area of Semberija to prevent them from defending themselves. So we found a way to leave the premises in order not to be confronted with much greater problems. Also on one other occasion when we went to the East Bosnia Corps command, we were intercepted by part of Mauzer's armed force. We had to flee through some side roads and also return through some side roads. I think that documents were compiled about that, too, and that you can still find them. The members of the Panthers went after us with an anti-aircraft cannon, but it overturned and one of them was even killed in that incident. In short, he was an absolute ruler of the Bijeljina municipality at the time, so there was no political support for us. Awhile later, I learned that before the war there were also certain tensions between Mr. Davidovic and Mr. Savic. You have to bear in mind that the two of them attended the same university in Sarajevo and their friendship dates from that period. And I think that all this contributed to my haste in a departure. I'll be quite open. To this very day, I'm angry at Mr. Stanisic. I never forgave him and I will not forgive him what he did to me. I did not request him to return me to my job, I simply wanted to see him and I requested that through his secretary, because at the time secretaries were far more powerful than centre chiefs. I wanted to speak about the problems and what happened. I looked for him in Belgrade, I looked for him at Pale. He was never there. He was always in the field. And I never had the opportunity to sit down to him and to speak to his face and to tell him, Mr. Minister, or Mico, the situation is not what you've been told. Mr. Kovac and other people told you something that is not true, under influence and pressure from Mr. Mauzer and others. I told you yesterday what I did. I told you that I did everything to the highest professional level. So I'm going to repeat it once again quite openly here in the courtroom: I never forgave Mr. Stanisic that he never received me and the fact that he did not listen to me. I wanted a formal, official commission by the MUP to be established to find out what happened and what did not happen. I'm telling you again very openly: I hope that some day I will have an opportunity to sit down with Mr. Stanisic and to discuss some of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you told us Mr. Stanisic was in Zvornik right after the Yellow Wasp operation and you were in a two-hour meeting where he was present, when was the next time after that that you saw him to speak with him, after early August 1992? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about dates again, but I'll skip the date. You check it in the documents. I said that Mr. Stanisic, while we were briefing him on our work and everything that we did, that he announced to us that there were similar or identical problems in other municipalities too. And in a way this was an announcement that the issue of paramilitarisation must be tackled elsewhere too. I don't know whether it was three or five or seven days later that Mr. Kljajic told me that Mr. Stanisic wanted to talk to me, and that's, I think, when Kljajic told me for the first time, in a friendly manner, Brother, you should establish a unit and go to Foca, but talk about these details with the minister who's waiting for you at the Bosanska Vila in Belgrade. The period between the first and the second meeting is one that I cannot accurately limit, because I'm bad when it comes to dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you were shown the document that your meeting with Mr. Stanisic at the Bosanska Vila in Belgrade took place on the 18th of August. If you accept that, can you tell me, when was the next time you saw and spoke with Mico Stanisic after that meeting in Belgrade when you talked about Foca? Did you see him or talk with him again in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. As I've just said, I was removed. And I tried to reach the minister through his secretary. I first observed the procedure, the procedure that was in place earlier, because you couldn't reach the minister directly. You had to go through the chief of the administration, and then he would check when the minister had time, and so on, but I skipped all that. I called up his office immediately, but he wasn't there. Leave a message, we'll get back to you; he is in the field; he's in Belgrade; he's not in Belgrade. And that's how it went. So I never met Stanisic again in 1992. I think that I didn't see him again until 1994, when he invited me to the Kikinda facility at Pale which I have mentioned already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us before about your meeting with Tomo Kovac where he told you that you had served your purpose and that they didn't want you anymore. Was that the only notice you got about your termination? Did you not get any paperwork from anyone indicating that you were being suspended or disciplined?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that I spoke to Mr. Kovac, as I have already described, and it is correct that I had done my job excellently. But I don't need to repeat the rest. He told me that I was suspended and that there was no need for me to come to work anymore. Then I insisted, because I know how much materiel was left behind in the gym. Those were items that were confiscated and certificates issued for that, and there were 150 motor cars that we confiscated and stored at the Radio Yugoslavia facility. I wanted to conduct a hand-over and make a record of it, and I believe that he accepted, and he initiated the setting up of a commission consisting of three persons. So I handed all this over and I was told that I needn't come to the MUP anymore and that I would be informed of any subsequent measures or activities. It is true, sir, that I never received a decision on my suspension. And I never received a decision on the institution of disciplinary proceedings. If you have anything to show to the contrary, I would like to see it. But I maintain that what I said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll return to that a little later on. I want to ask you, What did Mr. Kovac tell you about the reason you were being suspended? Did he mention the poker machine or did he just say that you weren't needed anymore?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've described the scene, and it's engraved in my memory for the rest of my life. He was surrounded by body-guards when I approached him. And although he was my superior, I didn't address him as Mr. Assistant or Comrade Assistant; I simply asked him, Tomo what is this supposed to mean? He simply said, You did a professional job, excellently, but we used you as a condom for -- as a disposable condom. That's all that Mr. Kovac said to me. I apologise for the language, but I simply quoted his words. And he didn't state any reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was his position at that time, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time he was assistant minister for the police. And let me try to clarify one more thing for you and the Trial Chamber. I wasn't necessary for Mr. Stanisic to suspend me or to institute disciplinary proceedings against me. I never received a decision in Bijeljina appointing me to the position of chief of the SJB or the CSB. I always had the status of police inspector at the police administration. I'll explain how it came about that I was treated as a SJB chief or CSB chief, but let me say this first: He planted a cuckoo's egg on Mr. Stanisic, like, have Mico bear the responsibility for me. But, in fact, legally speaking, if a suspension should have been imposed or disciplinary proceedings launched, it should have been him. He should have been the one to do that. And I owe you one more clarification about my appointments at the CSB and the SJB. As you know, pursuant to a decision of the minister and a dispatch, I arrived to Semberija and Majevica as an inspector, to conduct audits and provide professional help and other assistance. When I came to Bijeljina, the SJB was left without a chief, and we had coffee together every morning, whenever it was possible, and discussed work-related matters. I presented the problem to Mr. Kljajic. And I said, Cedo, the SJB cannot operate without a chief. And a Solomonic solution was found: All right, you do the work until we find somebody. That's how it was done. When we appointed the SJB chief and when that problem was solved, then we had the same kind of discussion again and I -- Mijic Davidovic said to Mr. Kljajic, Do appoint Dragan chief, at least temporarily; let him act as chief of the centre just as he acted as chief of the SJB until we find a new chief. So a decision of the minister was not required for my suspension or for disciplinary proceedings against me. That was the duty of Mr. Kovac as my superior at the police administration. I've already said that he had pulled out of it insidiously and put the blame on the minister. And then he said, Well, the -- it was the minister's orders. I tried -- I have tried to explain all aspects of these events to you. I may have used too many words in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or for me not enough, because I'm still lacking some understanding. You -- who had the authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings against you? Was it Mr. Kovac because he was assistant minister for police administration and you as an inspector were subordinate to him? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He was my superior officer. I never got an official decision about any appointment to an executive position, except for the position of police inspector. I was a member of the police administration and my superior officer was Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the time that you were serving as acting head of CSB in Bijeljina and head of SJB in Bijeljina, that was only on the oral say-so of Cedo Kljajic, right, the undersecretary for public security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if he requested approval from the minister, but I've already described how it went. Do take over the job until we find another solution. Yes, Mr. Undersecretary. I believe it was "Mr." already; it was no longer comrade. And then I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you get any kind of pay raise for being acting chief? Doesn't look like it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. And I'm not sure that the salary I was getting at the time was enough to pay for two boxes of cigarettes. It was ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So for all the hard work you did in Bijeljina and Brcko and Zvornik in trying to clean up the paramilitaries and get those stations running, your reward was you got suspended over a poker machine; is that a short summary of what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I would just like to add a remark; I would like to have it on the record once more: I did not take that poker machine without the approval of Undersecretary Cedo Kljajic, and the Official Note that you have says that pursuant to the approval of the undersecretary, the poker machine was taken from the storage. And I've already explained why I took it. When I was removed from my position, I also returned that poker machine. You never asked me about it, but I do want to add that. I and some five or six people who had come took some household appliances from the storage to use in the houses that were allotted to us. I also returned those household appliances that I had taken out of the storage, and I even went to buy 5 kilograms of washing soap because that was the quantity that I had taken out of our storage for my wife to be able to do the laundry for me and our kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just want to note that the page 75, line 15, when it starts after "a short summary what happened," and then "yes, sir" should be recorded as answer, and it was recorded as a question of you, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. And then the rest of it, following "yes, sir" is a continuation of his answer. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know that's important to you, Mr. Andan, and perhaps tomorrow before I finish I will return to ask you a couple of questions about it or documents related to that, but I want to go back to the Yellow Wasp operation for a moment. You're generally aware of the information that was obtained as a result of taking statements from all those Yellow Wasps who were arrested and detained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That requires clarification too. I've already said that we didn't have enough professionals to process those individuals adequately. Mr. Kljajic requested assistance from the minister to deploy some professionals, and that's when Mr. Goran Macar arrived in Bijeljina, who was chief of the crime police, and he was accompanied by half a dozen or maybe as many as ten inspectors who processed those individuals. I see that it isn't recorded anywhere, but the National Security Service also got involved. And apart from the crime aspect, the national security members from Zvornik interviewed Zuco and, I think, one or two more persons, but I don't know what they were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that some of the information that came out of these interviews indicated that Malko Koroman had been stopped at the check-point run by the Yellow Wasp at some point in time, I think transporting some Golf vehicles, and that subsequent to that Zuco and some of his men had gone to Pale and received weapons from the SJB in Pale and met with Mrs. Plavsic or Minister Subotic? Did you know about that information that came out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There has been a slight interpretation mistake again. The name is not "Marko" Koroman, it's "Malko" Koroman. But yes, I do have some information. I believe that Malko Koroman came to Zvornik from Pale with a very definite idea in his mind, that he and his friends be returned some cars that Zuco had earlier taken away at a check-point. As far as I remember the information, and to the extent it was available to me, the agreement was that the vehicles should be taken over and Zuco would get some quantity of weapons in return. I don't believe that the weapons that he needed could be found at the police station, so it had to go through a TO staff or it had to be taken from a military unit. I know, based on the information that was available to me then, that Zuco had set up contact with Ms. Plavsic, but, frankly speaking, I do not remember Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the information indicate that Zuco and his men had received weapons in Pale through the auspices of Mr. Koroman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did get the weapons that he had requested, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Koroman was subject to any disciplinary or criminal process related to this activity on his part?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because upon the completion of that operation, I left the ministry. I've already described the circumstances, or maybe we'll discuss it additionally, but that period to me is a black hole. I would prefer forgetting all about it, but I seem unable to. I don't know what happened to Malko Koroman later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us the other day, though, that you were aware that the minister had attempted to remove Malko Koroman. And I want to ask you, first of all, which minister are you referring to? Was that Mico Stanisic that tried to remove him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a request - I have digestive problems - I can answer this question, but if I could be excused later on, I would be grateful. Yes, I was referring to Mico Stanisic. I have already described that. He issued an order, written or oral, to replace Mr. Koroman. When the officials who were authorised to hand over that decision arrived at the Pale SJB, armed people gathered. I stated the number of 3.000. Well, that may be an exaggeration, but it was a large number of people. And they didn't allow that. They even chased out those people from the police station. They didn't allow Mr. Koroman to be removed. Immediately after that, Mr. Karadzic also got involved. And that's how Malko Koroman remained in his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there and ask that we take the break a minute or two early. And we'll resume tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we rise until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
